decks.title: Acids, Bases and Salts — Part 1: Acids, bases, indicators and their reactions
goals: Define acids and bases by the ions they give in water
Identify acids and bases with litmus, natural and olfactory indicators
Write equations for reactions of acids with metals, carbonates, hydrogencarbonates and bases
Explain why metal oxides are basic and non-metal oxides are acidic
Explain why acid solutions conduct electricity and why acid must be added to water

slides.heading: Acids, Bases and Salts
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what makes a substance an **acid** or a **base**, how **indicators** reveal them, how they react, and what happens to them in water.

visual.alt: Sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid react to give sodium chloride (common salt) and water
visual.caption: An acid and a base cancel each other out and leave a salt behind.

slides.narration: Namaste! Think of the sour bite of tamarind in sambar, the bitter taste of soap that slipped into your mouth, and the salt on your dining table. Sour things, soapy things and salts are linked by one big idea. In this lesson you will learn what makes a substance an acid or a base, how simple indicators reveal them, and how they react with metals, carbonates and each other. Let us begin.

slides.heading: Sour or soapy: two families of substances
slides.body_md: **Acids** taste sour. **Bases** taste bitter and feel soapy. In the laboratory we never taste or touch chemicals to identify them: many acids and bases are **corrosive**.

visual.alt: Table sorting common household items into acids and bases with the main substance in each

slides.narration: Your tongue already knows these two families. Lemon, tamarind, curd and vinegar taste sour because they contain acids. Soap solution tastes bitter and feels slippery because it is basic. The word acid comes from a Latin word meaning sour. But in a laboratory we never taste or touch a chemical to find out what it is. Strong acids and bases can burn skin and eyes. Chemists use a safer test instead, which we meet next.

slides.heading: Litmus: the classic indicator
slides.body_md: An **indicator** is a substance that shows, by a change of colour or smell, whether a solution is acidic or basic. **Litmus**, a purple dye from lichens, is the best known: acids turn blue litmus **red**; bases turn red litmus **blue**.

slides.narration: Litmus comes from lichens, the small crusty growths you see on rocks and old walls. Its solution is purple when neutral, and paper soaked in it is sold as blue and red strips. Dip blue litmus in lemon juice and the wet end turns red. Dip red litmus in soap solution and it turns blue. A simple way to remember: acids turn blue to red, bases turn red to blue. Neutral water changes neither strip.

slides.heading: Indicators from the lab and the kitchen
slides.body_md: Some indicators are made in laboratories; others come from plants. **Phenolphthalein** is colourless in acids and in neutral water, and turns **pink** only in bases.

visual.alt: Table of six indicators and their colours in acids and bases
visual.caption: Neutral colours: litmus is purple, methyl orange is orange, red cabbage extract is purple.

slides.narration: Here is your indicator chart. Methyl orange and phenolphthalein are made in laboratories. Phenolphthalein is the odd one: it stays colourless in acids and in neutral water, and turns pink only in a base. Turmeric, red cabbage and hibiscus petals are natural indicators you can try at home. Remember the yellow turmeric stain from dal on a white kurta? Scrub it with soap and it turns reddish-brown, because soap solution is basic.

slides.heading: Olfactory indicators: let your nose decide
slides.body_md: An **olfactory indicator** changes its **smell** in an acid or a base. Onion, vanilla essence and clove oil keep their smell in acids but **lose it in bases**. They let students with low vision test solutions too.

nodes.label: Cloth strip that smells of chopped onion

visual.alt: Flow: an onion-scented strip keeps its smell when acid is added but loses it when sodium hydroxide solution is added

slides.narration: Indicators do not always need eyes. Keep a few strips of clean cloth in a bag with chopped onion overnight. Next day, add a drop of dilute acid to one strip and a drop of dilute sodium hydroxide to another. The first strip still smells of onion; the second does not. Vanilla essence and clove oil behave the same way. Because they work through smell, these olfactory indicators let a student with low vision carry out the test independently.

slides.heading: Quick check: the turmeric stain
slides.body_md: A turmeric stain turns reddish-brown when it is scrubbed with soap. What does this tell you?
slides.narration: Time for a quick check. Look at what happened to the turmeric stain, and recall which family of substances turns turmeric reddish-brown. Then pick the option that matches. Read the explanation afterwards, even if you are sure you got it right.

slides.body_md: Zinc granules in dilute sulphuric acid give off a gas. Led into soap solution, it fills bubbles that burst with a **pop** near a flame: the gas is **hydrogen**.

slides.narration: Watch zinc granules in dilute sulphuric acid. Tiny bubbles stream off the metal. We lead the gas through a delivery tube into soap solution, where it blows soap bubbles. Bring a burning candle near a rising bubble and it bursts with a small pop. That pop is the signature of hydrogen gas. Never bring the flame close to the test tube itself, because hydrogen mixed with air can explode.

slides.heading: Acid plus metal gives salt plus hydrogen
slides.body_md: General pattern: **acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas**. The metal takes the place of hydrogen in the acid.

visual.alt: Zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid give zinc chloride and hydrogen gas
visual.caption: This is why pickles and chutneys are stored in glass or ceramic jars, not metal tins.

slides.narration: Every reaction of this kind follows one pattern. The metal pushes hydrogen out of the acid and takes its place, forming a salt. With sulphuric acid, zinc forms zinc sulphate. With hydrochloric acid, it forms zinc chloride. This is also why Nani never stores lemon pickle or tamarind chutney in an iron or aluminium tin. The acids would slowly attack the metal and spoil both the food and the container. Glass and ceramic jars are safe.

slides.heading: Some bases react with metals too
slides.body_md: Zinc warmed with sodium hydroxide solution gives **sodium zincate** and hydrogen. Only a few metals, such as zinc and aluminium, react with bases like this.

visual.alt: Sodium hydroxide and zinc give sodium zincate and hydrogen gas
visual.caption: The gas again burns with a pop.

slides.narration: Here is a surprise. Hydrogen also forms when zinc granules are warmed with sodium hydroxide solution. The salt formed is called sodium zincate. Does that make sodium hydroxide an acid? No. It still turns red litmus blue and feels soapy. Only a few metals, such as zinc and aluminium, react with bases this way. If an exam asks about this reaction, name both products: sodium zincate and hydrogen.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: magnesium in hydrochloric acid
slides.body_md: Riya drops a clean magnesium ribbon into dilute hydrochloric acid. Predict the products and write the balanced equation.
bullets: Step 1 — recognise the pattern: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
Step 2 — name the salt: magnesium forms $\ce{Mg^2+}$, so it needs two $\ce{Cl-}$ ions: magnesium chloride, $\ce{MgCl2}$.
Step 3 — skeletal equation: $\ce{Mg + HCl -> MgCl2 + H2}$.
Step 4 — chlorine is 1 on the left and 2 on the right, so write 2 before HCl: $\ce{Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2}$.
Step 5 — check: Mg 1 = 1, H 2 = 2, Cl 2 = 2. Confirm the gas with the pop test.

visual.alt: Atom check: one magnesium, two hydrogen and two chlorine atoms on each side of the balanced equation

slides.narration: Let us predict before we write. Magnesium is a metal and hydrochloric acid is an acid, so we expect a salt and hydrogen. Magnesium ions carry a charge of two plus, so the chloride needs two chloride ions: magnesium chloride. Write the skeletal equation, then count. Chlorine is one on the left and two on the right, so place a two before hydrochloric acid. That balances hydrogen too. Finally, confirm the gas: a pop near a flame means hydrogen.

slides.body_md: Dilute hydrochloric acid on sodium carbonate fizzes. The gas turns **lime water** (calcium hydroxide solution) **milky**: it is **carbon dioxide**. Hydrogencarbonates react the same way.

slides.narration: Now try a carbonate. Pour dilute hydrochloric acid onto sodium carbonate in a test tube and cork it quickly. The gas travels through the delivery tube and bubbles into clear lime water, which soon turns milky. That milkiness is the test for carbon dioxide. Every metal carbonate and hydrogencarbonate reacts with acids like this, giving a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Marble chips and limestone are calcium carbonate, so they fizz in acid too.

slides.heading: Why lime water turns milky, then clear again
slides.body_md: Carbon dioxide forms insoluble **calcium carbonate**: the milkiness. With **excess** carbon dioxide, soluble **calcium hydrogencarbonate** forms and the liquid clears.

visual.alt: Flow: clear lime water turns milky with some carbon dioxide and clears again with excess carbon dioxide

slides.narration: Why milky? Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate, a white solid that does not dissolve. Its tiny particles make the liquid look like watered-down milk. Keep bubbling the gas and the milkiness disappears. The extra carbon dioxide and water turn calcium carbonate into calcium hydrogencarbonate, which does dissolve. So if a question says the gas is passed for a long time, describe both stages.

slides.heading: Quick check: fizzing baking soda
slides.body_md: Baking soda and vinegar fizz when mixed. Which test identifies the gas?
slides.narration: Here is a quick check. Baking soda is a hydrogencarbonate and vinegar is an acid. Think about which gas this pair must produce, and then the test that proves it. Choose your option and read the explanation.

slides.heading: Neutralisation: acid and base cancel out
slides.body_md: **Acid + base → salt + water.** Add dilute hydrochloric acid drop by drop to sodium hydroxide solution made pink with phenolphthalein. When the pink just disappears, the base has been **neutralised**.

edges.label: add dilute acid drop by drop
add one or two drops of base

visual.alt: Flow: pink sodium hydroxide with phenolphthalein turns colourless when enough acid is added, and pink again when a little base is added

slides.narration: Picture this in your school lab. A flask of sodium hydroxide with a few drops of phenolphthalein is pink. Add dilute hydrochloric acid drop by drop while swirling. Suddenly the pink vanishes: the acid has used up all the base. That is neutralisation, and the products are a salt and water. Add one more drop of base and the pink returns. An acid and a base cancel each other, like a debit and a credit in a bank passbook.

slides.heading: Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic
slides.body_md: An oxide tells you about the element it comes from.
columns:
**Metal oxide + acid → salt + water**

Black copper(II) oxide dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid and the solution turns **blue-green**.

$\ce{CuO + 2HCl -> CuCl2 + H2O}$

So metal oxides behave as **bases**.

**Non-metal oxide + base → salt + water**

Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide (lime water).

$\ce{Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O}$

So non-metal oxides behave as **acids**.
slides.narration: Oxides give away the nature of their element. Warm a pinch of black copper oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid and it dissolves, leaving a blue-green solution of copper chloride. Salt plus water: exactly what a base gives with an acid. So metal oxides are basic. Carbon dioxide, an oxide of the non-metal carbon, reacts with a base like lime water, again giving a salt and water. So non-metal oxides are acidic. Metal oxide pairs with acid; non-metal oxide pairs with base.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how an antacid works
slides.body_md: Arjun takes milk of magnesia, magnesium hydroxide, for acidity. Write the reaction with stomach acid and name its type.
bullets: Step 1 — identify: magnesium hydroxide is a base; stomach acid is hydrochloric acid.
Step 2 — type: acid + base → salt + water, so this is **neutralisation**.
Step 3 — skeletal equation: $\ce{Mg(OH)2 + HCl -> MgCl2 + H2O}$.
Step 4 — balance Cl with $\ce{2HCl}$, then H and O with $\ce{2H2O}$: $\ce{Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + 2H2O}$.
Step 5 — check: Mg 1 = 1, O 2 = 2, H 4 = 4, Cl 2 = 2.

visual.alt: Atom check for the antacid reaction: one magnesium, two oxygen, four hydrogen and two chlorine atoms on each side

slides.narration: Arjun ate too much spicy food and feels a burning in his chest. His stomach has made extra hydrochloric acid. Milk of magnesia is a mild base, magnesium hydroxide. Acid plus base gives salt plus water, so this is neutralisation. Write the skeletal equation, balance chlorine with two hydrochloric acid, then hydrogen and oxygen with two water. Count every element once more. A mild base is chosen because a strong base would harm the food pipe and stomach.

slides.heading: Quick check: black powder in acid
slides.body_md: What do you see when copper(II) oxide is warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid, and what does it show?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the colour of the solution that forms, and about what kind of oxide copper oxide is. Remember the pairing rule from two slides ago. Choose your answer, then read why the other options do not fit.

slides.heading: What all acids share: hydrogen ions
slides.body_md: Acid solutions **conduct electricity**; glucose and alcohol solutions do not, though they also contain hydrogen. In water, acids produce **hydrogen ions**, $\ce{H+}$, and moving ions carry the current.

slides.narration: Fix two iron nails in a rubber cork, stand them in a beaker, and connect them to a bulb and a six volt battery. Pour in dilute hydrochloric acid and the bulb glows. Try glucose solution or alcohol and it stays dark. Glucose and alcohol contain hydrogen too, so why the difference? Acids split up in water to give hydrogen ions, and moving ions carry electric current. It is hydrogen ions, not just hydrogen atoms, that make a substance an acid.

slides.heading: Hydronium ions, hydroxide ions and alkalis
bullets: A hydrogen ion cannot exist alone in water; it joins a water molecule: $\ce{H+ + H2O -> H3O+}$, the **hydronium ion**.
Bases give **hydroxide ions** in water: $\ce{NaOH(s) ->[water] Na+(aq) + OH-(aq)}$.
A base that dissolves in water is an **alkali**, e.g. $\ce{NaOH}$, $\ce{KOH}$. Not all bases dissolve.
Dry hydrogen chloride gas does **not** turn dry blue litmus red: no water, no ions.

visual.alt: Hydrogen chloride in water gives hydronium ions and chloride ions

slides.narration: A lone hydrogen ion is too small and too reactive to float about by itself. It attaches at once to a water molecule, making a hydronium ion. Bases do the opposite job: they release hydroxide ions in water. Bases that dissolve in water have a special name, alkalis. Here is a neat test of the idea. Dry hydrogen chloride gas does nothing to dry blue litmus paper. Moisten the paper and it turns red at once, because now there is water to form ions.

slides.heading: Diluting safely: always acid into water
slides.body_md: Mixing a concentrated acid with water is **highly exothermic**. Add the acid **slowly to water**, stirring all the time. Adding water to concentrated acid can make the mixture boil and splash, and the glass may crack.

visual.caption: Safety: wear goggles. Always add acid to water, never water to concentrated acid.

slides.narration: Diluting an acid releases a lot of heat. Pour water into concentrated sulphuric acid and the first few drops heat up so fast that the mixture can boil and spit acid at your hands and face. The container may even crack. So the safe order is always acid into water: a thin stream of acid into plenty of water, stirred constantly, so the heat spreads out. Dilution also lowers the number of ions in each millilitre of solution.

slides.body_md: Read the assertion and the reason about diluting sulphuric acid.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red and give $\ce{H+}$ ions (as $\ce{H3O+}$) in water.
Bases taste bitter, feel soapy, turn red litmus blue and give $\ce{OH-}$ ions in water; bases that dissolve in water are alkalis.
Indicators: litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein, turmeric, red cabbage, hibiscus; olfactory: onion, vanilla, clove oil.
Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.
Dilute by adding acid to water, never the reverse.

rows: Indicator changes colour at the end point

visual.alt: Summary table of the reactions of acids and bases with their products and the sign or test for each

slides.narration: Let us pull Part 1 together. Acids are sour and give hydrogen ions in water. Bases are bitter and soapy and give hydroxide ions. Indicators, whether litmus, turmeric or an onion strip, tell them apart. Acids react with metals to give hydrogen, with carbonates to give carbon dioxide, and with bases and metal oxides to give a salt and water. Read the table aloud once, especially the test for each gas. And always, acid into water.

slides.heading: Exam tips: acids and bases
bullets: Name the gas **and** its test: hydrogen — burns with a pop; carbon dioxide — turns lime water milky.
Write salt formulae carefully: $\ce{MgCl2}$, not $\ce{MgCl}$; $\ce{Na2SO4}$, not $\ce{NaSO4}$.
Zinc with sodium hydroxide gives sodium zincate, $\ce{Na2ZnO2}$, and hydrogen.
"Acid to water" — and give the reason: a lot of heat is released.
Explain conductivity with **ions**, not just "acids contain hydrogen".
A typical 3-mark reaction answer: observation (1) + balanced equation (1) + gas test or reaction type (1).
slides.narration: Here is how to collect every mark. When you name a gas, add its test. Write salt formulae carefully: magnesium chloride has two chlorines and sodium sulphate has two sodiums. Learn the unusual one, zinc with sodium hydroxide, giving sodium zincate. For dilution, the reason matters as much as the rule: heat is released. When explaining why acids conduct, talk about ions. And in a three-mark question, examiners look for an observation, a balanced equation and a test or type.

slides.heading: How acidic? How basic?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — measuring acidity with the **pH scale**, why pH matters in your body, your mouth and your fields, and what **salts** are.

visual.alt: Flow along the pH scale: acidic below 7, neutral at 7, basic above 7

slides.narration: Welcome back. In Part 1 you learnt to tell an acid from a base. Now we ask a sharper question: how acidic, or how basic? Doctors ask about acidity, dentists warn about sweets, and farmers test their soil, and all three are really talking about one number, called pH. By the end of this part you will read that number with confidence and also understand the salts that acids and bases leave behind.

slides.heading: Strong and weak acids and bases
slides.body_md: **Strength** depends on how many ions a substance gives in water. At the same concentration, a **strong acid** gives many $\ce{H+}$ ions; a **weak acid** gives few.
bullets: **Concentrated** means much acid in little water; **strong** means it splits almost completely into ions. The two words are not the same.

visual.alt: Table of common strong and weak acids and bases

slides.narration: Strong and concentrated sound alike, but they mean different things. Concentrated means a lot of acid in a little water. Strong means the acid splits almost completely into ions. Hydrochloric acid on your lab shelf is a strong acid. The acetic acid in vinegar is weak: even in a pickle jar it gives only a few hydrogen ions. Bases work the same way: sodium hydroxide is strong, while ammonium hydroxide is weak.

slides.heading: The pH scale: from 0 to 14
slides.body_md: **pH** tells how acidic or basic a solution is. pH 7 is **neutral**, below 7 is **acidic** and above 7 is **basic**. The **more** hydrogen ions a solution has, the **lower** its pH.

visual.caption: Values are approximate. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is basic.

slides.narration: The p in pH comes from potenz, the German word for power. Read the scale like a number line. Seven, in the middle, is neutral, like pure water. Moving left, solutions get more acidic and hold more hydrogen ions; gastric juice in your stomach sits near one and a half. Moving right, solutions get more basic, up to sodium hydroxide near fourteen. Remember the flip: more hydrogen ions means a lower pH number.

slides.heading: Universal indicator: many colours, one number
slides.body_md: **Universal indicator** is a **mixture** of indicators. It shows a different colour at each pH, so it tells **how** acidic or basic a solution is, not just which family it belongs to.

visual.alt: Table of typical universal indicator colours: red for strongly acidic, orange to yellow for weakly acidic, green for neutral, blue for weakly basic and violet for strongly basic
visual.caption: Shades vary between brands; always match against the chart on the bottle.

slides.narration: Litmus answers only one question: acid or base? Universal indicator answers a better one: how acidic, or how basic? It is a mixture of several indicators, so it passes through a rainbow of colours across the scale. Add a few drops to a sample, or dip a strip of pH paper, and compare the colour with the chart printed on the bottle. Red means strongly acidic, green means neutral and violet means strongly basic.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ranking four samples by pH
slides.body_md: Kavya adds universal indicator to four samples. **A** turns red, **B** green, **C** blue and **D** orange. Arrange them in increasing order of pH and find the one with the most hydrogen ions.
bullets: Step 1 — turn colours into approximate pH: A red, about 1; D orange, about 4; B green, 7; C blue, about 9.
Step 2 — increasing pH: A < D < B < C.
Step 3 — most hydrogen ions means lowest pH: **A**.
Step 4 — classify: A and D acidic, B neutral, C basic.
Check — as pH rises along the order, the hydrogen-ion concentration falls.

visual.alt: Four samples arranged in increasing pH from their universal indicator colours: A red, D orange, B green, C blue

slides.narration: Kavya's results look like a traffic signal gone wild, but the colour chart tames them. Red means about one, orange about four, green exactly seven and blue about nine. Now line them up from the smallest pH to the largest: A, then D, then B, then C. The sample with the most hydrogen ions has the lowest pH, so the answer is A. Always finish by checking that your order runs the right way.

slides.body_md: Four solutions have pH 2, 6, 7 and 11. Which one has the highest concentration of hydrogen ions?
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember the flip we met on the pH scale: what happens to the pH number as hydrogen ions increase? Use that to choose. Then read the explanation.

slides.heading: pH inside your body
slides.body_md: Our body works within a narrow pH range of about **7.0 to 7.8**. The stomach makes **hydrochloric acid**, which helps digestion. Too much acid causes pain and irritation; an **antacid**, a mild base such as **milk of magnesia** (magnesium hydroxide), neutralises the excess.

nodes.label: Extra hydrochloric acid in the stomach
Antacid, a mild base, neutralises the extra acid

visual.alt: Flow: a heavy meal leads to extra stomach acid and pain, which an antacid relieves by neutralisation

slides.narration: Your body is fussy about pH. Blood stays slightly basic, around seven point four, and cells work only in a narrow range. Your stomach, though, keeps hydrochloric acid on purpose, because it helps digest food. After a heavy wedding feast the stomach may make too much acid, and you feel a burning pain that people call acidity. An antacid, a mild base like milk of magnesia, neutralises the extra acid and brings relief.

slides.heading: Tooth decay starts below pH 5.5
slides.body_md: **Tooth enamel**, made of calcium hydroxyapatite (a calcium phosphate), is the hardest substance in the body, but it corrodes when the pH in the mouth falls **below 5.5**. Bacteria turn sugar and food left in the mouth into **acids**. Basic toothpastes neutralise them.

series.label: Typical pH after a sugary snack

visual.alt: Graph of pH on the tooth surface after a sugary snack: it falls from about 6.8 to about 5.0 within ten minutes, stays below the critical value of 5.5 for roughly twenty minutes, and climbs back to about 6.7 by one hour
visual.caption: A typical pattern; exact values vary from person to person.

slides.narration: Here is what happens on your teeth after a sweet. Within minutes, bacteria feed on the sugar and make acids, and the pH on the tooth surface dives below five point five. Below that line, enamel slowly dissolves. Saliva brings the pH back up, but that takes half an hour or more. Nibbling sweets all day keeps teeth below the line for hours. That is why rinsing after meals and brushing with a basic toothpaste protects your teeth.

slides.heading: Soil pH and farming
slides.body_md: Plants grow well only in a particular range of soil pH. **Too acidic** soil is treated with bases such as **slaked lime** or powdered limestone; **too basic** soil is improved with **organic matter** such as compost, which releases acids as it decays.

rows: Add slaked lime or powdered limestone
Add compost or other organic matter

visual.alt: Table linking soil pH to crop growth and the usual remedy
visual.caption: Tea is an exception: it prefers acidic soil, as in the hills of Assam and Darjeeling.

slides.narration: Many farmers in India receive a Soil Health Card that lists the pH of their field. Most crops like soil that is close to neutral. If the soil is too acidic, the farmer spreads slaked lime or powdered limestone, both bases. If it is too basic, compost helps, because decaying organic matter releases acids. Tea is a famous exception: it loves acidic soil, which is one reason it grows so well in Assam and Darjeeling.

slides.heading: Acid rain harms rivers and monuments
slides.body_md: Rain with a pH **below 5.6** is called **acid rain**. It forms when oxides of sulphur and nitrogen from burning fuels dissolve in rainwater. Lakes and rivers turn acidic, which makes survival hard for fish, and marble is slowly eaten away.

nodes.label: Smoke from factories and vehicles: oxides of sulphur and nitrogen
Oxides dissolve in rain: pH below 5.6
Lakes and rivers turn acidic: fish suffer

visual.alt: Flow: sulphur and nitrogen oxides from smoke dissolve in rain to make acid rain, which acidifies lakes and corrodes marble

slides.narration: Normal rain is slightly acidic, because some carbon dioxide dissolves in it. But smoke from power plants, factories and vehicles adds oxides of sulphur and nitrogen. These dissolve in rain to form acids, and when the pH drops below five point six we call it acid rain. It flows into lakes and rivers and makes life hard for fish. It also attacks marble, which is one reason polluting industries are restricted near the Taj Mahal.

slides.heading: Stings, bites and natural remedies
slides.body_md: Some animals and plants defend themselves with acids, and a **mild base** neutralises them.

rows: An acid that causes pain and irritation
A mild base such as baking soda
A mild base such as baking soda
Rubbing with the leaf of the dock plant

visual.alt: Table of stings and bites that inject acids and the mild bases used to relieve them

slides.narration: Nature uses acids as weapons. A honeybee sting leaves an acid that causes pain and swelling, and red ants inject methanoic acid, also called formic acid. A paste of baking soda, a mild base, neutralises the acid and eases the pain. The nettle plant of the hills has stinging hairs that inject methanoic acid; its traditional remedy, the dock plant, often grows nearby. Wash a sting first, and see a doctor if swelling spreads.

slides.body_md: Below which pH does tooth enamel start to corrode?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think back to the graph of pH on the tooth surface and the dashed line on it. Pick the value that marks the danger zone, then read the explanation.

slides.heading: What is a salt? Salt families
slides.body_md: A **salt** forms when an acid reacts with a base. Its positive part comes from the **base** and its negative part from the **acid**. Salts that share a positive or a negative part belong to one **family**.

visual.alt: Table of five salts with their parent acids, parent bases and the families they belong to

slides.narration: In chemistry, salt does not mean only the white powder in the salt shaker. A salt is any compound formed when an acid and a base neutralise each other. To find its parents, split the salt in two. The metal or ammonium part comes from the base, and the rest comes from the acid. Salts that share a part form a family: sodium chloride and sodium sulphate are sodium salts, while sodium chloride and potassium chloride are both chlorides.

slides.heading: Is every salt solution neutral?
slides.body_md: No. The pH of a salt solution depends on the **strength of its parent acid and base**.

visual.alt: Table: strong acid and strong base give a neutral salt, strong acid and weak base an acidic salt, weak acid and strong base a basic salt

slides.narration: Here is a rule that earns marks. Think of a tug of war between the parent acid and the parent base. If both are strong, they cancel out and the salt solution is neutral, like sodium chloride. If the acid is the stronger parent, the solution is acidic, like ammonium chloride. If the base is stronger, the solution is basic, like sodium carbonate. So to predict the pH of a salt, first name its parents, then judge their strength.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting the pH of salt solutions
slides.body_md: Predict whether solutions of ammonium nitrate, potassium sulphate and sodium acetate are acidic, basic or neutral.
bullets: Step 1 — ammonium nitrate, $\ce{NH4NO3}$: nitric acid (strong) + ammonium hydroxide (weak), so **acidic**, pH below 7.
Step 2 — potassium sulphate, $\ce{K2SO4}$: sulphuric acid (strong) + potassium hydroxide (strong), so **neutral**, pH 7.
Step 3 — sodium acetate, $\ce{CH3COONa}$: acetic acid (weak) + sodium hydroxide (strong), so **basic**, pH above 7.
Check — universal indicator should show a yellowish, a green and a bluish colour.

visual.alt: Worked table predicting that ammonium nitrate is acidic, potassium sulphate neutral and sodium acetate basic from the strength of their parents

slides.narration: Let us use the tug of war. Ammonium nitrate comes from nitric acid, which is strong, and ammonium hydroxide, which is weak. The acid wins, so the solution is acidic. Potassium sulphate has two strong parents, so it is neutral. Sodium acetate comes from weak acetic acid and strong sodium hydroxide, so the base wins and the solution is basic. Ammonium nitrate is a common fertiliser, so this reasoning even helps farmers.

slides.heading: Quick check: which salt solution is basic?
slides.body_md: Which of these salts gives a basic solution in water?
slides.narration: Quick check. For each salt, name the parent acid and the parent base, and decide which parent is stronger. The basic solution comes from the salt whose base wins the tug of war.

slides.narration: Copper sulphate crystals look perfectly dry, yet they contain water. Heat a few in a dry test tube and watch. The blue colour fades to white, and droplets of water appear near the cooler mouth of the tube. That water was locked inside the crystals: five water molecules for every unit of copper sulphate. It is called water of crystallisation, and it gives the crystals their blue colour and their shape.

slides.heading: Add water, and the blue comes back
slides.body_md: White **anhydrous** copper sulphate turns blue again when water is added. Other hydrated salts: **gypsum**, $\ce{CaSO4.2H2O}$, and **washing soda**, $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$.

visual.alt: White anhydrous copper sulphate takes up water and becomes blue hydrated copper sulphate
visual.caption: White to blue on adding a liquid is a quick test for water.

slides.narration: Now cool the white powder and add a few drops of water. It turns blue again and becomes warm. The change works both ways: heat drives the water out, and water brings the colour back. That is why white anhydrous copper sulphate is used to check whether a liquid contains water. Gypsum holds two water molecules per formula unit and washing soda holds ten. Keep these three numbers ready: five, two and ten.

slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about anhydrous copper sulphate is true or false.
slides.narration: Last check for this part. Think about what the word anhydrous means, and what colour you saw at the bottom of the hot test tube. Then decide.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: pH runs from 0 to 14: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; more $\ce{H+}$ ions means lower pH.
Strong acids and bases give many ions; weak ones give few. Universal indicator shows the pH by colour.
pH matters: body pH 7.0–7.8, antacids, tooth decay below 5.5, soil treatment, acid rain below 5.6, stings.
A salt's solution can be acidic, basic or neutral, depending on the strength of its parents.
Hydrated salts: $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ (blue), $\ce{CaSO4.2H2O}$ (gypsum), $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$ (washing soda).

rows: Mouth: tooth enamel starts to corrode
Pure water; salts of a strong acid and a strong base
Range in which the human body works

visual.alt: Summary table of important pH values and where they occur

slides.narration: Let us wrap up Part 2. The pH scale runs from zero to fourteen, with seven as neutral, and more hydrogen ions mean a lower number. Universal indicator turns that number into a colour. pH decides whether your stomach feels fine, whether your teeth decay and whether a crop grows well. Salts can be acidic, basic or neutral depending on their parents. And hydrated salts hold water of crystallisation: five, two and ten.

slides.heading: Exam tips: pH and salts
bullets: "Higher pH" means **less** acidic. Do not say a pH 2 solution is weaker than a pH 5 one.
Strong ≠ concentrated: define strength by how many ions form.
To predict a salt's pH, write the parent acid and base with their strengths — this step usually carries a mark.
Tooth decay: state "below pH 5.5" and name the cause (bacteria make acids from sugar).
Write hydrates with a dot: $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$; "anhydrous" means without water of crystallisation.
Antacid answers need the word **neutralise** and an example such as milk of magnesia.
slides.narration: Here are the traps examiners love. A higher pH means less acidic, not more. Strong and concentrated are different words, so define strength by the number of ions. When you predict the pH of a salt, write its parents and their strengths: that step usually earns a mark. For tooth decay, give the number five point five and the cause. Write hydrated salts with a dot. And whenever an antacid appears, use the word neutralise.

slides.heading: Chemicals from common salt
slides.body_md: Part 3 — how one cheap raw material, **sodium chloride**, becomes sodium hydroxide, bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda, plus **plaster of Paris** from gypsum.

edges.label: with ammonia, carbon dioxide and water

visual.alt: Route map: common salt gives sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen by electrolysis; chlorine gives bleaching powder; salt also gives baking soda, which gives washing soda

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 3. Sodium chloride is the salt in your kitchen, but it is also one of the most important raw materials in industry. From brine, factories make sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen. From those, they make bleaching powder. From salt, ammonia and carbon dioxide, they make baking soda, and from baking soda, washing soda. We will also meet plaster of Paris, made from gypsum. Keep this route map in mind as we go.

slides.heading: Where common salt comes from
slides.body_md: **Sea water** is evaporated in shallow salt pans. **Rock salt** is mined from beds left where ancient seas dried up. Crude salt contains impurities and is purified before use.

slides.narration: India makes most of its salt from the sea. Along the coasts of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, sea water is let into shallow pans. The sun and wind evaporate the water, the brine gets saltier, and white crystals form, which salt workers rake into heaps. Rock salt, or sendha namak, comes from beds left behind when ancient seas dried up; India has rock salt mines in Himachal Pradesh. Crude salt is purified before it reaches your table.

slides.body_md: Passing electricity through **brine**, a concentrated solution of sodium chloride, gives **chlorine** at the anode, **hydrogen** at the cathode and **sodium hydroxide** solution near the cathode.

slides.narration: Now let us split salt with electricity. Brine is a concentrated solution of common salt in water. When a direct current flows through it, chlorine gas bubbles off at the anode, the positive electrode. Hydrogen gas bubbles off at the cathode, the negative electrode. And the solution near the cathode slowly becomes sodium hydroxide. One raw material gives three useful products, which is why chlor-alkali plants, such as those around Bharuch in Gujarat, are so important.

slides.heading: Why it is called the chlor-alkali process
slides.body_md: **Chlor** for chlorine, **alkali** for sodium hydroxide.
bullets: Anode (+): chlorine gas
Cathode (−): hydrogen gas
Near the cathode: sodium hydroxide solution
Atom check: Na 2 = 2, Cl 2 = 2, H 4 = 4, O 2 = 2

visual.alt: Brine and electricity give sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen
visual.caption: Balanced: two sodium, two chlorine, four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms on each side.

slides.narration: The name tells the story. Chlor stands for chlorine, and alkali stands for sodium hydroxide, the two main products. Look at the equation: two units of sodium chloride and two of water give two of sodium hydroxide, one chlorine molecule and one hydrogen molecule. Count with me: two sodium, two chlorine, four hydrogen and two oxygen on each side. Learn this equation well; it appears in board papers often.

slides.heading: Three products, many uses
slides.body_md: Hydrogen and chlorine can also be combined to make **hydrochloric acid**.

rows: Fuel; making ammonia for fertilisers; hardening oils into vanaspati and margarine
Disinfecting water and swimming pools; making PVC, disinfectants and pesticides; making bleaching powder
Cleaning steel; making medicines and cosmetics; making ammonium chloride
Making soaps, detergents and paper; making artificial fibres; removing grease from metals

visual.alt: Table of uses of hydrogen, chlorine, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide from the chlor-alkali process

slides.narration: Each product finds work. Hydrogen is a clean fuel, makes ammonia for fertilisers and hardens vegetable oils into vanaspati. Chlorine keeps drinking water and swimming pools free of germs and goes into PVC pipes and pesticides. Burn hydrogen in chlorine and you get hydrogen chloride, which dissolves in water to make hydrochloric acid for cleaning steel. Sodium hydroxide makes soaps, detergents and paper. Your morning bath may depend on this one plant.

slides.heading: Quick check: which gas, which electrode?
slides.body_md: In the electrolysis of brine, which gas is given off at the anode?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the diagram of the brine cell, and which electrode is positive. Then think about which gas bubbled up there. Choose your answer.

slides.heading: Bleaching powder
slides.body_md: Passing **chlorine** over **dry slaked lime** gives **bleaching powder**. It is usually written as $\ce{CaOCl2}$, though its real composition is more complex.

visual.alt: Slaked lime and chlorine give bleaching powder and water
visual.caption: Bleaching powder smells of chlorine and should be stored in a closed container.

slides.narration: Here is our first chemical made from chlorine. Chlorine gas is passed over dry slaked lime, which is calcium hydroxide, and a pale yellow-white powder forms. That is bleaching powder. Its formula is usually written as calcium oxychloride, though the real substance is a mixture. Open a pack and you will smell chlorine, because it slowly releases the gas. That chlorine is what kills germs and removes colours.

slides.heading: Uses of bleaching powder
slides.body_md: Bleaching powder is a strong **oxidising agent** and **disinfectant**.

rows: Water works, wells and village tanks
Makes drinking water free of germs

visual.alt: Table of five uses of bleaching powder: disinfecting water, bleaching cotton, linen, wood pulp and laundry, and as an oxidising agent

slides.narration: After a flood in Assam or Bihar, health workers often add measured amounts of bleaching powder to wells and tanks, because floodwater spreads germs that cause cholera and typhoid. Textile mills use it to whiten cotton and linen, paper mills to whiten wood pulp, and laundries to brighten clothes. In factories it also works as an oxidising agent. Handle it with care: it can burn skin and fade coloured clothes.

slides.heading: Baking soda: sodium hydrogencarbonate
slides.body_md: **Baking soda**, $\ce{NaHCO3}$, is made from sodium chloride, water, carbon dioxide and ammonia. It is a **mild, non-corrosive base**.
bullets: Used in baking powder
An ingredient in antacids
Used in soda-acid fire extinguishers

spec.equation: NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 -> NH4Cl + NaHCO3

visual.alt: Sodium chloride, water, carbon dioxide and ammonia give ammonium chloride and sodium hydrogencarbonate

slides.narration: The white powder called meetha soda in many kitchens is sodium hydrogencarbonate. Factories make it by passing carbon dioxide and ammonia through a cold solution of common salt; ammonium chloride forms as well. Baking soda is a mild base, so it does not burn the skin. That is why it is safe in food, in antacids for an upset stomach, and in soda-acid fire extinguishers, where it reacts with an acid to release carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Why cakes and dhoklas rise
slides.body_md: On heating, baking soda gives **carbon dioxide**, which puffs up the batter. **Baking powder** is baking soda mixed with a mild edible acid such as **tartaric acid**; the acid adds more carbon dioxide and neutralises the bitter-tasting sodium carbonate.

nodes.label: Baking powder: baking soda + tartaric acid
Water and heat in the batter

visual.alt: Flow: baking powder in a wet, warm batter releases carbon dioxide bubbles that make the cake or dhokla soft and spongy

slides.narration: Why is a good dhokla so spongy? When baking powder gets wet and warm, the tartaric acid reacts with the baking soda and releases carbon dioxide. Thousands of tiny bubbles get trapped in the batter, which rises and sets soft and spongy. If you used only baking soda, heating would still make some gas, but it would leave behind sodium carbonate, which tastes bitter. The acid in baking powder prevents that.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: heating baking soda
slides.body_md: Meera heats baking soda in a dry test tube. Write the balanced equation and explain why a cake made with only baking soda can taste bitter.
bullets: Step 1 — reactant: sodium hydrogencarbonate; products: sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide.
Step 2 — skeletal equation: $\ce{NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2}$.
Step 3 — sodium is 1 on the left and 2 on the right, so write 2 before $\ce{NaHCO3}$: $\ce{2NaHCO3 ->[heat] Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2}$.
Step 4 — check: Na 2 = 2, H 2 = 2, C 2 = 2, O 6 = 6.
Step 5 — the leftover sodium carbonate is a stronger base with a bitter taste; the acid in baking powder neutralises it.

visual.alt: Atom check for heating baking soda: two sodium, two hydrogen, two carbon and six oxygen atoms on each side

slides.narration: Let us follow Meera's test tube. Baking soda breaks down on heating into sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. In the skeletal equation, sodium is one on the left but two on the right, so we put a two before baking soda. Now count hydrogen, carbon and oxygen: all match. The sodium carbonate left behind is a stronger base and tastes bitter. That is exactly why bakers use baking powder, with its edible acid, instead of plain baking soda.

slides.heading: Washing soda
slides.body_md: Heating baking soda gives sodium carbonate. **Recrystallising** sodium carbonate from water gives **washing soda**, $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$, a basic salt.
bullets: Making glass, soap and paper
Making borax
A cleaning agent at home
Removing **permanent hardness** of water

visual.alt: Sodium carbonate takes up ten water molecules to form washing soda crystals

slides.narration: Washing soda is sodium carbonate with ten water molecules of crystallisation. Dissolve sodium carbonate in water and let it crystallise, and you get these colourless crystals. Glass, soap and paper factories use it in bulk, and it is used to make borax. At home, a spoonful helps remove greasy stains. It also removes permanent hardness of water, so soap lathers better. Do not confuse it with baking soda: one cleans, the other cooks.

slides.heading: Quick check: baking soda or washing soda?
slides.body_md: Choose the correct statement about these two sodium salts.
slides.narration: Quick check. Two sodas, two very different jobs. Recall each formula, whether it contains water of crystallisation, and where each one is used. Then choose.

slides.heading: Plaster of Paris from gypsum
slides.body_md: Heating **gypsum** at **373 K** removes most of its water of crystallisation and gives **plaster of Paris**, calcium sulphate hemihydrate. Overheating removes all the water, and the product no longer sets well.

visual.alt: Gypsum heated at 373 K gives plaster of Paris and water
visual.caption: Two formula units of calcium sulphate share one water molecule in plaster of Paris.

slides.narration: Next, a salt that hardens like stone. Gypsum is calcium sulphate with two water molecules. Heat it gently, to three hundred and seventy three kelvin, which is the boiling point of water, and it loses most of that water. What remains is plaster of Paris, a fine white powder. In it, two units of calcium sulphate share one water molecule, which is why its formula shows a half. Heat it too strongly and it will not set properly.

slides.heading: Setting: back to gypsum
slides.body_md: Mixed with water, plaster of Paris turns back into **gypsum** and sets into a **hard solid mass** within minutes.
bullets: Plaster casts for broken bones
Toys, statues and decorative mouldings
Smoothing walls and making false ceilings

nodes.label: Plaster of Paris: fine white powder

visual.alt: Flow: gypsum heated at 373 K becomes plaster of Paris, which sets back into a hard mass of gypsum when mixed with water

slides.narration: Watch a doctor set a broken wrist. A bandage soaked in plaster of Paris paste is wrapped around the arm, and within minutes it hardens into a stiff cast. The powder has taken back water and turned into interlocking gypsum crystals. Sculptors use the same reaction for statues and toys, and builders use it for smooth walls and false ceilings. Because it reacts with water, the dry powder must be stored in moisture-proof containers.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting water in a plaster cast
slides.body_md: How many water molecules are taken up when two formula units of plaster of Paris set into gypsum?
bullets: Step 1 — plaster of Paris is $\ce{CaSO4.1/2H2O}$, so two formula units hold **1** water molecule.
Step 2 — gypsum is $\ce{CaSO4.2H2O}$, so two formula units hold **4** water molecules.
Step 3 — water taken up = 4 − 1 = **3 molecules** (one and a half per formula unit).
Step 4 — whole-number equation: $\ce{(CaSO4)2.H2O + 3H2O -> 2CaSO4.2H2O}$.
Step 5 — check: Ca 2 = 2, S 2 = 2, O 12 = 12, H 8 = 8.

visual.alt: Table: two units of plaster of Paris hold one water molecule, two units of gypsum hold four, so three water molecules are taken up on setting

slides.narration: Fractions in formulas confuse many students, so let us count with whole numbers. Take two units of plaster of Paris: together they hold one water molecule. Two units of gypsum hold two each, so four in total. The difference, three molecules, is the water the plaster takes up as it sets. That is one and a half per formula unit, matching the equation on the earlier slide. Always check that your atoms balance.

slides.heading: Quick check: storing plaster of Paris
slides.body_md: Read the assertion and the reason about storing plaster of Paris.
slides.narration: Final check. Think about what plaster of Paris does when it meets water, and what moist air contains. Judge the assertion, then the reason, then the link between them.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 3
bullets: Common salt comes from sea water and rock salt.
Electrolysis of brine gives chlorine (anode), hydrogen (cathode) and sodium hydroxide (near the cathode).
Bleaching powder: chlorine + dry slaked lime. Baking soda: salt + water + carbon dioxide + ammonia.
Washing soda: recrystallised sodium carbonate, $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$.
Plaster of Paris: gypsum heated at 373 K; sets with water back into gypsum.

visual.alt: Summary table of five chemicals with formula, raw material and one use each

slides.narration: Let us wrap up the chapter. Common salt from the sea or from rock salt mines is split by electricity into sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen. Chlorine and slaked lime give bleaching powder. Salt, ammonia and carbon dioxide give baking soda, and baking soda leads to washing soda. Gypsum gives plaster of Paris, which sets back into gypsum. Read the table aloud: name, formula, raw material and one use for each.

slides.heading: Exam tips: chemicals from common salt
bullets: Chlor-alkali: chlorine at the **anode**, hydrogen at the **cathode**, sodium hydroxide **near the cathode** — learn the balanced equation.
Baking soda $\ce{NaHCO3}$ vs washing soda $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$: do not swap the formulae.
Plaster of Paris is $\ce{CaSO4.1/2H2O}$, made at **373 K**; gypsum is $\ce{CaSO4.2H2O}$.
"Why store plaster of Paris in a moisture-proof container?" — it reacts with water and sets.
"Why does baking powder contain tartaric acid?" — it neutralises bitter sodium carbonate and adds carbon dioxide.
A 3-mark "preparation" answer: raw materials (1) + balanced equation (1) + two uses (1).
slides.narration: Here is how to score full marks. In the chlor-alkali process, say where each product forms, and write the balanced equation. Never swap the formulae of baking soda and washing soda. For plaster of Paris, write the half water and the temperature, three hundred and seventy three kelvin. Learn the two favourite why-questions: storing plaster away from moisture, and the role of tartaric acid. And for preparation questions, give raw materials, an equation and two uses.

notes.title: Acids, Bases and Salts — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Acids, bases and indicators
sections.body_md:
**Acids** taste sour, turn blue litmus red and give hydrogen ions, $\ce{H+}$, in water. **Bases** taste bitter, feel soapy, turn red litmus blue and give hydroxide ions, $\ce{OH-}$, in water. Never taste or touch laboratory chemicals.

**Indicators** show by a change of colour (or smell) whether a solution is acidic or basic.
- **Litmus** (from lichens; purple when neutral): acid → red, base → blue.
- **Synthetic indicators:** methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base); phenolphthalein (colourless in acid and neutral solution, pink in base).
- **Natural indicators:** turmeric (reddish-brown in base, no change in acid), red cabbage extract, hibiscus (gudhal) petals.
- **Olfactory indicators** change smell: onion, vanilla essence and clove oil lose their smell in a base but keep it in an acid.

**Natural sources of acids:** citric acid (lemon, orange), tartaric acid (tamarind), lactic acid (curd), acetic acid (vinegar), methanoic acid (ant and nettle stings).

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that gives hydrogen ions ($\ce{H+}$, present as $\ce{H3O+}$) in water; sour, turns blue litmus red.
A substance that gives hydroxide ions ($\ce{OH-}$) in water or neutralises an acid; bitter and soapy.
A substance whose colour (or smell) depends on whether a solution is acidic or basic.
An indicator whose smell changes in an acid or a base, e.g. onion, vanilla, clove oil.

| Reaction | General pattern | Test / observation |
|---|---|---|
| Acid + metal | salt + hydrogen | gas burns with a pop |

sections.heading: 3. Acids and bases in water; dilution
sections.body_md:
- All acids contain hydrogen, but not every hydrogen compound is an acid: **glucose** and **alcohol** solutions do not conduct electricity and are not acidic.
- Acid solutions **conduct electricity** because they contain ions. The $\ce{H+}$ ion cannot exist alone; it joins water to form the **hydronium ion**, $\ce{H3O+}$.
- **Dry** hydrogen chloride gas does not change **dry** blue litmus; acidic behaviour needs water.
- Bases give $\ce{OH-}$ ions in water. Bases that dissolve in water are **alkalis** (e.g. $\ce{NaOH}$, $\ce{KOH}$, $\ce{NH4OH}$); not all bases dissolve.
- **Dilution** (mixing an acid or base with water) lowers the concentration of ions per unit volume. It is **highly exothermic**: always add **acid to water** slowly with constant stirring. Adding water to concentrated acid can make the mixture boil and splash, and the container may crack.

key_terms.definition_md: $\ce{H3O+}$, formed when a hydrogen ion joins a water molecule.
A base that dissolves in water.
Mixing an acid or base with water, which lowers the concentration of ions per unit volume.

sections.heading: 4. Strength of acids and bases: the pH scale
sections.body_md:
- **pH** is a scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or basic a solution is: **7 neutral**, **below 7 acidic**, **above 7 basic**.
- The **higher** the concentration of $\ce{H+}$ ions, the **lower** the pH. Moving from 7 up to 14, the concentration of $\ce{OH-}$ ions increases.
- **Universal indicator** is a mixture of indicators that shows a different colour at different pH values, so it gives an approximate pH.
- **Strong acids** (hydrochloric, sulphuric, nitric) give many $\ce{H+}$ ions; **weak acids** (acetic, citric, carbonic) give few, at the same concentration. **Strong bases**: sodium and potassium hydroxide; **weak base**: ammonium hydroxide.
- **Strong** (degree of ionisation) is not the same as **concentrated** (amount of acid per volume of solution).

A mixture of indicators that shows different colours across the pH scale.
An acid that gives a large number of hydrogen ions in water, e.g. hydrochloric acid.
An acid that gives relatively few hydrogen ions in water, e.g. acetic acid.

sections.heading: 5. Importance of pH in everyday life
sections.body_md:
- **Plants and animals:** living things survive only in a narrow pH range; the human body works at about **pH 7.0 to 7.8**. **Acid rain** (pH below **5.6**) makes rivers and lakes acidic and harms aquatic life.
- **Soil:** plants need a suitable soil pH. Acidic soil is treated with slaked lime or powdered limestone; basic soil with organic matter.
- **Digestion:** the stomach makes **hydrochloric acid** to help digestion. Excess acid causes pain and irritation; **antacids** such as milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide), mild bases, neutralise it.
- **Tooth decay** starts when the pH in the mouth falls **below 5.5**. Bacteria turn sugar and food particles into acids, which corrode **enamel** (calcium hydroxyapatite, the hardest substance in the body). Basic toothpastes neutralise the acid.
- **Self-defence by animals and plants:** bee stings leave an acid; ants and nettle hairs inject **methanoic acid**. A mild base such as baking soda gives relief; the dock plant is a traditional remedy for nettle stings.

key_terms.definition_md: A mild base, such as magnesium hydroxide, taken to neutralise excess stomach acid.
Rain with a pH below 5.6, caused by oxides of sulphur and nitrogen dissolving in rainwater.
Calcium hydroxyapatite; corrodes when mouth pH falls below 5.5.

sections.heading: 6. Salts: families, pH and water of crystallisation
sections.body_md:
- A **salt** is formed when an acid reacts with a base. The positive part comes from the base; the negative part from the acid. Salts sharing a positive or negative part form a **family** (sodium salts; chloride salts).
- **pH of salt solutions:** strong acid + strong base → **neutral** ($\ce{NaCl}$, $\ce{K2SO4}$); strong acid + weak base → **acidic** ($\ce{NH4Cl}$); weak acid + strong base → **basic** ($\ce{Na2CO3}$, $\ce{NaHCO3}$, $\ce{CH3COONa}$).
- **Water of crystallisation** is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt. Blue $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ turns **white** (anhydrous) on heating and blue again when water is added. Gypsum is $\ce{CaSO4.2H2O}$; washing soda is $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A compound formed when an acid reacts with a base.
Salts having the same positive or the same negative part, e.g. NaCl and Na₂SO₄ (sodium family).

sections.heading: 7. Chemicals from common salt
sections.body_md:
**Common salt** is obtained by evaporating sea water and by mining **rock salt**.

**Sodium hydroxide (chlor-alkali process):** electrolysis of brine gives chlorine at the **anode**, hydrogen at the **cathode** and sodium hydroxide **near the cathode**. Uses — hydrogen: fuels, ammonia for fertilisers, hardening oils; chlorine: water treatment, PVC, disinfectants, pesticides, bleaching powder; HCl: cleaning steel, medicines; NaOH: soaps, detergents, paper, artificial fibres, degreasing metals.

**Bleaching powder** ($\ce{CaOCl2}$): chlorine on dry slaked lime. Uses: bleaching cotton, linen, wood pulp and laundry; oxidising agent; disinfecting drinking water.

**Baking soda** ($\ce{NaHCO3}$): from salt, water, carbon dioxide and ammonia. A mild non-corrosive base. On heating gives sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. **Baking powder** = baking soda + mild edible acid (tartaric acid). Uses: baking, antacids, soda-acid fire extinguishers.

**Washing soda** ($\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$): recrystallised sodium carbonate. Uses: glass, soap and paper industries; making borax; cleaning; removing permanent hardness of water.

**Plaster of Paris** ($\ce{CaSO4.1/2H2O}$): gypsum heated at **373 K**. Sets with water into hard gypsum. Uses: casts for fractures, toys, decorative materials, smoothing surfaces. Store in moisture-proof containers.
